new.title: Stand before a Roman-era Egyptian temple in Leiden
new.desc: The Temple of Taffeh, built in Nubia under Emperor Augustus, was a thank-you gift from Egypt for Dutch help in saving monuments from the Aswan dam. It was rebuilt block by block in the central hall of the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden.
new.tip: The hall was designed so you can see the temple before you reach the ticket desk, so even a quick stop on the way through Leiden counts.

new.title: Look Trix the T. rex in the eye at Naturalis
new.desc: Leiden's natural history museum is home to Trix, one of the most complete Tyrannosaurus skeletons ever found and one of only two real tyrannosaurs on permanent display in Europe.
new.tip: Naturalis is a short walk from Leiden Centraal, behind the LUMC hospital. Book a timed slot online on school holidays.

new.title: Walk the ring wall of the Burcht van Leiden
new.desc: An artificial hill where the Old and New Rhine meet, crowned by a round medieval keep that is a thousand years old. From the top of the wall you look out over the rooftops to the Hooglandse Kerk.
new.tip: Enter through the iron gate on Burgsteeg and look up at the stone lion above the inner gate. Brasserie Rumour at the foot of the hill is good for a drink afterwards.

new.title: Climb inside Molen De Valk, Leiden's last city windmill
new.desc: Leiden once had nineteen windmills along its ramparts; De Valk is the only one left standing in the old city. It is now a museum where you climb floor by floor up to the stage around the sails.
new.tip: Combine it with a stroll along the Galgewater just behind it, one of the most photographed corners of Leiden.

new.title: Hunt for wall poems around Leiden
new.desc: Since 1992 more than a hundred poems in their original languages have been painted on Leiden's house walls, from Tsvetaeva in Russian to a haiku by Bashō. Turning a corner and finding one is half the fun.
new.tip: Start at Bashō on Rapenburg near the Hortus and download one of the free self-guided routes; the translations are online too.

new.title: Slip through a door into a Leiden hofje
new.desc: Behind plain doors all over Leiden hide some 35 hofjes: quiet courtyards ringed by almshouses, some centuries old. The Jean Pesijnhofje beside the Pieterskerk stands where Pilgrim Father John Robinson once lived.
new.tip: Most hofjes are free to enter during the day, but people live there, so keep your voice down. The tourist office sells a map of them.

new.title: Sit in Einstein's chair at Leiden's Old Observatory
new.desc: The Oude Sterrewacht at the edge of the Hortus is one of the oldest university observatories in the world. Its visitor centre shows the history of Dutch astronomy and one dome holds the chair Einstein used during his visits.
new.tip: Look out for the public open evenings, when you can climb to the domes and look through the old telescopes if the sky is clear.

new.title: Have a beer under the original Heineken star in Leiden
new.desc: De Vergulde Kruik has been pouring since 1881, with stained glass and old silver taps. Local legend says Heineken's red star came from a sign in this brown café.
new.tip: Ask the bar staff for their version of the star story; there is more than one and they enjoy telling it.

new.title: Eat the Hollandaise at Café Visscher in Leiden
new.desc: A Bib Gourmand bistro on Stationsweg where chef Arie Visscher keeps things simple and seasonal. Leidenaars come for the steak tartare and the famous Hollandaise.
new.tip: It is right between the station and the centre, so it works for a long lunch before the train home. Grab a seat in the conservatory.

new.title: Learn the tulip's story at De Zwarte Tulp in Lisse
new.desc: This small museum in the heart of the Bollenstreek tells how bulbs from Turkey became the region's whole economy, with old tools, paintings of bulb fields and tulip-decorated silver and porcelain.
new.tip: A good rainy-day plan B on a Keukenhof trip; it is in the village centre and much quieter. There is a guided tour on Sundays.

new.title: Find Countess Jacoba's castle ruin at Teylingen
new.desc: Between Voorhout and Sassenheim stands the moated ruin of Slot Teylingen, a 13th-century castle where Countess Jacoba van Beieren spent her last years. Its round wall and keep rise straight out of the bulb fields.
new.tip: The grounds close for winter, but the ruin is easy to admire from the lane around it. Pair it with a spring bulb-field ride from Lisse.

new.title: Visit Duivenvoorde, the castle that was never sold
new.desc: First mentioned in 1226, Kasteel Duivenvoorde in Voorschoten has only ever passed down through inheritance. Inside are family portraits and Delftware; outside an English landscape park with a moat, old trees and kingfishers.
new.tip: The park is open daily for a small walking fee, and Paviljoen Duivenvoorde serves lunch with produce from the estate. Buses stop right on the driveway.

new.title: Visit Huygens' country house Hofwijck in Voorburg
new.desc: Constantijn Huygens designed this little house in a square pond in 1640, and his son Christiaan, who discovered Saturn's ring, spent his last years here. The garden was rebuilt to the original plan.
new.tip: It is right next to Voorburg station; in the 19th century part of the garden was given up for the railway. Look out for the old ice cellar.

new.title: See Katwijk's White Church and its 1605 beacon
new.desc: The Witte Kerk stands right on Katwijk's boulevard, saved in WWII when a contractor told to demolish it only took down the tower. Just behind it is the Vuurbaak, a fishermen's beacon from 1605 and one of the oldest lighthouses in the country.
new.tip: The beacon can be climbed on summer open days for a view over dunes and sea. Listen out for Katwijks, the local dialect, while you walk the boulevard.

new.title: Dinner at Neefies, Katwijk's tiny local favourite
new.desc: A small restaurant a hundred steps from the boulevard, with generous plates, plenty of fish and a menu full of jokes in the Katwijks dialect.
new.tip: It is small and open evenings only, so book ahead and walk to the beach for sunset afterwards.
new.q: Neefies E.A. Borgerstraat Katwijk aan Zee

new.title: Go underground in the Atlantikwall bunkers at Noordwijk
new.desc: In the dunes south of Noordwijk lie the bunkers of the German Batterie Noordwijk, linked by tunnels that volunteers have opened up. You visit the fire control bunker and can join a tour through the underground corridors.
new.tip: Only open in summer, as bats hibernate in the tunnels in winter. Book the tunnel tour online and park at Wantveld rather than on busy Bosweg.

new.title: Step into a Soyuz at Space Expo in Noordwijk
new.desc: Space Expo is the visitor centre of ESA's technical heart ESTEC, so the real European space programme is right next door. Inside: a replica ISS, a Soyuz simulator and André Kuipers' story.
new.tip: On weekends and holidays there is a tour into the actual ESTEC test halls; it sells out, so book it with your ticket.

new.title: Pancakes at Boerderij Meijendel in the Wassenaar dunes
new.desc: An old farm in the middle of the Meijendel dunes, now a big self-service pancake house with a terrace and a fireplace for cold days. The classic reward after a dune walk.
new.tip: Start at De Tapuit, Dunea's visitor centre next door, where several short walks of 3 to 5 km begin.

new.title: Taste farm-made Leidse kaas on Kaag island
new.desc: De Kaagse Boer is a working dairy farm from 1850 on the island of Kaag that still makes red-rinded Leidse kaas with the pressed keys. It also has a small cheese museum.
new.tip: Cycle there and cross on the little ferry from Buitenkaag; bring some cash for the island.

new.title: Take the little ferry to Kaag island
new.desc: Kaag is an island village in the middle of the Kagerplassen, the lake district north of Leiden. A small ferry from Buitenkaag gets you across, and then it is water views, sails and waterside terraces.
new.tip: Want to go further? Rent a sloep in Warmond; no boating licence is needed for the small electric ones.

new.title: Ski indoors on real snow in Zoetermeer
new.desc: SnowWorld Zoetermeer has had real snow since 1996, and its longest slope runs 300 metres down a hall more than 70 metres tall.
new.tip: Beginners start on the two short slopes; finish with fondue in the après-ski restaurant. RandstadRail from Den Haag CS gets you to Zoetermeer.

new.title: Feed the lorikeets at Avifauna in Alphen aan den Rijn
new.desc: Avifauna is the Netherlands' big bird park, with more than 230 species from flamingos to penguins. In the lorikeet aviary the birds land on you for nectar.
new.tip: Check the day's schedule for the bird demonstrations and plan your route around them. No need to book, and you can bring your own picnic.
new.q: Vogelpark Avifauna Alphen aan den Rijn

new.title: See how the Westland became one big greenhouse
new.desc: The Westlands Museum in Honselersdijk tells how this corner became the world's largest greenhouse horticulture area. Behind the farmhouse is a garden with an old grape greenhouse and a fruit wall that once kept vines warm.
new.tip: Leave time for the garden; volunteers tend it daily and the old glasshouses are the highlight. It is an easy bike ride from Den Haag through the greenhouse landscape.

new.title: Buy Frankenthaler grapes at Sonnehoeck in Kwintsheul
new.desc: Before tomatoes and flowers, the Westland was known for table grapes grown under glass. Sonnehoeck is a historic grape nursery, now a national monument, still growing Frankenthalers the traditional way.
new.tip: In season the grapes are sold at the stall on Saturday mornings while stock lasts. Come early and look at the 1815 fruit wall.

new.title: Find where the Pilgrims left Leiden for America
new.desc: Leiden sheltered the English Pilgrims for eleven years before they left in 1620. A statue and plaque on the Vliet mark where they boarded a river barge to Delfshaven, the first leg of the journey that ended with the Mayflower.
new.tip: Walk on to the Pieterskerk, where a plaque honours their pastor John Robinson, who is buried there.
